body_markdown:
I haven’t counted the hours that I have into[Project Cheap Camaro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/project-cheap-camaro-8-sneaking-up-on-color) , but it’s safe to call the effort so far “substantial.” The hours have been such that when I’m *not* welding, spraying, or sanding, I really ought to be doing something—anything—other than thinking about the car.


But if you’re reading this, you already know that’s not how it works. Project cars invade your mental space just as much as they do your physical space. Using the word “obsession” sounds too clinical, so let’s just call it a healthy addiction. I figure my interest level is just on the downhill side of required intervention: There may be hushed tones overheard from family members in the next room, but so far no action.


They may think this addiction is madness, but I’d counter that there’s method to it: If the first layer of a project is hands-on work, such as paint or welding or building an engine, then there’s an underlying layer that works to keep the whole process moving forward. That’s the motivation behind coming in from working on the car all afternoon only to doomscroll on your phone for missing bits and pieces. You won’t need those parts for a year or three, but you will *need* them.


Your teen daughter’s watching *Dance Moms* for the umpteenth time? Look for an axle on Marketplace. National news got you down? Maybe there’s an oil pan on Craigslist. And while you’re in there… might as well check on eBay Motors. See? It makes sense.


For the same reason I don’t count the hours I have into this project, I *do* count the first time one of these “needs” actually paid off: rear window trim.


## Fit Check!


If you remember the[welding sparks era of Cheap Camaro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/project-cheap-camaro-make-mine-a-coupe/) , you’ll recall the sorta-correct quarter panel fit exercise. Left and right-side full quarters of questionable origin came with the car. Did they fit? It depends on how you define “fit.” In the end, they worked, though, but it didn’t dawn on me until later that with no rear window trim to use as a fit check at the rear glass area, I had a problem on my hands.


The trim hadn’t come with the car, and I was planning on just sourcing a set after paint. At least, until I really thought about it.


That trim is designed to fit snug to the contour of the body, where my hacked-up roof skin met the who-knows-from-where sourced quarter panels. Eventually, I figured out that any problems with that contour in the body would be obvious once the trim was installed.


So while I was sanding the Eastwood polyester high-build primer during the day, I was spending my evenings hunting for OEM Camaro rear window trim so I could check out how close to correct my Cheap Camaro’s body really was.


When I was fitting sheetmetal, I wasn’t really paying attention to the fine details. But those upper corners where the roof met the new quarters? Yeah, they’re not quite right—and I didn’t think about that until it was almost too late to do something about it.


Jim Pickering


I didn’t want reproduction trim—one less variable, I figured, considering how many problems I smoothed out to make all this sheet metal into a proper Camaro-like shape. No, it was original or nothing, but finding a set of rear window trim turned out to be harder than I expected. You’d think that a collector car as popular as a first-gen Camaro would yield better results, but that wasn’t the case. I looked online for weeks. Wandered swap meets. Aftermarket parts were available, sure, but when it came to OEM stainless, no luck.


But I’ve learned this process is a lot like fishing. Sometimes you just have to wait.


The solution came one afternoon from my enabler father (he’ll sit on my side of the room in any forthcoming classic car intervention). The phone rings, and it’s him. “Camaro window trim,” he says. “Just popped up on Marketplace. $100. Looks original.”


I pulled up the listing and sized it up: This OEM stuff was cheaper than reproduction and close-ish in terms of distance away. So I ended up mini road-tripping on a Tuesday afternoon to check it out.


Martin was the seller’s name, and he runs a Mopar parts business that focuses on B- and E-body Chryslers from the muscle era. Somewhere along the line some OEM first-gen Camaro trim found its way into his stash. The stainless was complete and nice enough to be worth the money he was asking, so I picked it up. When I asked about all the cars on the property and the business of Mopar, Martin told me about a big-block E-body he had just pulled out of a field out by the Oregon Coast. “Just about rusted in half,” he said. “They’re still out there.”


My kind of guy.


There are a lot of good aftermarket window trim solutions for Camaro, but for this car, I needed original stainless trim to make sure the body shape was really on the money.


Jim Pickering


When I found a good set, I mocked it up on the car to see how far off the roof really was compared to the original shape. Here I’ve already used a little bit of filler to fix the corners and have mocked up the complete trim set with masking tape to check the fit after the fix. See the tan-colored filler? That’s how far off the roof was from where it should have been. It may seem like a small correction, but inconsistent gaps really stand out.


Jim Pickering


In the end, it didn’t take much to fix the few wide spots I had where the trim met the roof, but it would have driven me nuts for years had I just gone straight to paint without checking this fit first. It’s important to do this before any 2K urethane primer work, as filler shouldn’t be applied on top of your primer surfacer.


Jim Pickering


I got home and held the OEM trim up to the Camaro’s body. Sure enough, the fit wasn’t really a fit. I had an inconsistent curvature and gaps that I never would have seen without that trim in hand—and once the car was painted, there’d be no way to fix it. But with the car still in primer, I did fix it, and now everything lines up as it should.


## Picking up Speed


That trim situation was a convenient win that immediately got me thinking: *You never know when you might actually need some of the missing stuff.* So, I got to hunting other things from Cheap Camaro’s parts list while *Dance Moms* was on. I started with an oil pan for the 427 big-block, as[we’d smashed the original one](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/project-cheap-camaro-7-big-block-or-bust/) . No luck, at least not locally. So I moved that to the back burner and started in on a transmission.


Does an unpainted car with no running engine really need a transmission? Yes, it does.


Cheap Camaro was originally a floor-shift manual car. Although I have the four-speed pedals, I’ve been building this car as a nice driver with my wife in mind, and she’d prefer it have an automatic. That ruled out the glory of an M22 Rock Crusher four-speed. Instead, I started looking for GM Turbo-Hydramatic 400s on Marketplace.


The Turbo 400, introduced in 1964, was GM’s go-to three-speed automatic. It is legendary in terms of brute strength, but GM quit building them in the 1990s, and most of what you find for sale on the used market today came out of no-miles motorhomes or million-mile trucks. There are a bunch of variants out there, too: switch-pitch versions; two different bellhousing patterns; long and short tail housings; and more. The ones I initially found for sale had truck-style bolt-on yokes. One looked like it had been pulled out of a swamp. Even the easy stuff isn’t always easy: For anything other than an expensive aftermarket rebuild, it was a waiting game again.


After about a month of watching, I found a listing for a short-tailshaft, Chevy-bolt pattern TH400 from a seller I happened to know—a guy named Lonnie who runs an auto shop named Carolina Customs. Asking price: $200.


This $200 TH400 transmission is supposedly a low-miles unit, but there’s no telling how hard those miles were. The only evidence I have is what I saw from the last mile: pictures of big-block carnage that ended this car’s party. Think I’ll have to rebuild it?


Jim Pickering


Lonnie said the transmission came out of a Chevelle. The story went that the owner had spun a couple of bearings in his big-block, but that the transmission was a low-mileage unit and it seemed fine. I got the sense that it probably still worked, but it came with no guarantee. Carolina Customs’ fix for that car was an LS swap and modern overdrive automatic, so the TH400 was now homeless. And sure enough, when I made the 20-mile drive to Lonnie’s shop out by the Portland airport, the transmission was on the floor next to a Chevelle.


Notice I said “probably” worked. But the 400’s fluid was still red and smelled OK, and Lonnie handed me a small-diameter torque converter that came as part of the deal. “3500-or-so stall,” he said, which conjured images of my wife’s “nice driver” 427 Camaro wheel-standing off the line at the dragstrip like one of Grumpy’s Toys.


The input shaft turned freely and the pump seal hadn’t been leaking, which is a good sign. I still need to pull the oil pan off and check the filter, but I’ll deal with that on a rainy day. Worst case: garage rebuild.


Jim Pickering


GM TH400s had ID tags riveted to the passenger’s side of the case, and this one’s still there. The printing is gone but the stampings remain: 465 means April 9, 1968, production. CD code suggests big-block 396/350 Chevelle application.


Jim Pickering


But who can argue with $200? I paid the man, loaded up the 400 and brought it home for a good cleaning. Maybe it’ll need a rebuild, maybe it won’t, but the whole thing seemed worth the gamble.


After I muscled the transmission onto a wheeled cart in my driveway, I noticed it still had its riveted tag on the side of the case, which had some specific ID numbers: CD-68. According to that, this transmission was probably behind a 350-horsepower 396-cubic-inch big-block in a ’68 Chevelle. Score one for Cheap Camaro: a factory big-block trans from the right year. I stuck it under the bench for later.


## Chasing Bits


You’d think Edelbrock Performer RPM intake manifolds would be easy to find used, but it took me a while to source this oval-port piece. Torker IIs? Performer 2-Os? They’re everywhere. Goes to show that the stuff that really works well for street performance is usually kept versus sold—and stuff is always available when you *don’t* need it.


Jim Pickering


I feel like I’ve been all over the area to source stuff for this car. Beyond Oregon City and the Portland airport, I’ve crossed the Columbia River into Washington for an Edelbrock Performer RPM intake manifold for oval-port big-block Chevrolets, from a lady named Joanna. I had to sandblast it to remove some black oxidation, but it was worth the $100 I spent. I drove right past the *Spruce Goose* in McMinnville, Oregon, for a big-block-specific Camaro TH400 transmission crossmember, from a guy named Steve. He also had a set of transmission cooler lines and sold me all of it for $125. I missed out on a set of OEM front window trim when the seller accidentally drove over it with his truck before I could make the several-hour trek. And just this past weekend, I drove 50 miles down to Salem to meet a guy named Joe, who himself was at one time building a 427 Camaro. A new-in-box six-quart oil pan was all he had left from that project. For $100, it came home with me.


Hunting for the transmission taught me something I didn’t know: Chevrolet had to offset the big-block engine in Camaros about an inch or so to the passenger’s side, which meant that the TH400 crossmember for big-block Camaros had to be offset, too. This one came from a guy named Steve, who told me he swapped out the TH400 in his ’67 Camaro for an M22 Rock Crusher four-speed.


Jim Pickering


I can visualize the complete car: It’s just been blown apart, with bits sprinkled all over the Portland Metro area. Covering distance and meeting people is just part of the game. I can only imagine how hard this would all be if I were building Project Cheap AMX, but the hunt is part of the adventure, even if the hours it takes don’t make much sense to those around me.


But I know something they don’t: After that first wheel stand, I won’t be the only one in need of an intervention.
